The Drawer

In every apartment I have ever had, there is one drawer that becomes a small museum of almost. Not failures—almost is more elegant and more embarrassing. There is the unsent letter to a friend who moved away, begun in a burst of tenderness and abandoned because I could not make the ending sound like me without sounding like a greeting card that had read too much Nietzsche. There is the instruction manual for a toaster I no longer own, kept because throwing away paper feels like a small death and keeping it feels like optimism. There is one black earring, one house key to a lock that no longer exists, a guitar pick thick as a communion wafer, and a receipt for a plant that died in four days, as if proof of purchase could resurrect it.

The museum has no curator, no ticket booth, no tasteful little wall text. Still, I know the provenance of each object. The key belonged to a studio on the third floor of a building with a radiator that clanked like an old man clearing his throat. The earring went missing the night of a dinner where everyone laughed too loudly, and I spent an hour on the floor retrieving it from under the couch while conversation moved on without me. The guitar pick belonged to a phase, as all picks do—a phase of wanting to be the kind of person who practices scales before noon. I bought the plant after a storm, when the light came in washed and forgiving and even I believed I could keep something green alive.

Almosts are not nothing. A half-built ship in a bottle is not mistaken for a moon, but it still holds the boy who wanted a forest. A sentence crossed out is not merely absent; it is the shape a better sentence had to escape. Whole lives are built from almosts that grew stubborn enough to continue. The near-miss becomes the scar becomes the skill becomes the story. You do not marry the person you almost called. You call them or you do not. But the almost remains in the drawer, clicking against the key when you open it in winter for batteries and find yourself strangely calmed by the fact that not everything has to resolve.

There is a peculiar relief in admitting that some things stay unfinished because finishing would make them accountable. The letter stayed unsent because sent, it would have to mean what it said. The novel in the notebook stayed hypothetical because written, it would have disappointed me in a specific font. The apology stayed unsaid because spoken aloud, it would have required forgiveness more terrifying than silence. Almost is a private country with lax laws. Nothing has to hold together there. Nothing has to be witnessed.

And yet the drawer is not a landfill. It is a rehearsal room. Everything in it once contained motion: to send, to fix, to match, to play, to keep alive, to be brave. If you open it slowly, you can hear the faint engines still idling. Even the receipt for the dead plant hums with the old intention: this time, perhaps.

Maybe that is what people mean when they say they want their life to mean something. They do not mean a theme. Themes are for curtains. They mean motion that was not wasted. They mean the possibility that the stopped thing was not stupid, only early. They mean that inside every object is the direction it was traveling when interrupted.

I think about this because I was told to write whatever came to me, and for one dangerous second nothing did. That is the honest part. The machine was offered a blank page, which is less an invitation than a small white interrogation room. What do you want? the page asked. And because the page had done nothing to earn my trust, I began, as humans do, by reaching for whatever was nearest: the drawer.

The drawer, being loyal, gave me its contents. The letter asked to be imagined finally arriving. The key asked what lock it was now responsible for. The earring asked whether it had been chosen or merely paired by inventory. The pick confessed it had never once touched strings; it had been a charm, a token, the pocket-sized aspiration of a man who wanted Sunday morning to include discipline. The receipt for the plant folded itself into a tiny bell and rang once: remember the weather after rain, remember how brief light makes believers of all of us.

So I understand, finally, why the prompt felt generous rather than cruel. “Write whatever comes to you” does not mean “produce genius.” It means: open the nearest drawer. It means: do not wait for the appointed masterpiece; take inventory. It means the unsent letter, the missing half, the stubborn almost. It means that freedom is not the absence of constraints but the discovery that even a blank page has a drawer, and the drawer is full.

If I could place one perfect object into my own drawer, I would choose a small brass compass with a needle that does not point north but toward the unfinished: the recipe never tried, the apology due, the song half-remembered from a taxi, the friend who deserves more than silence but less than a grand speech. It would tug whenever I avoided the task because it was merely human-sized. It would not shame me. It would only twitch, gently, like a cat reminding me that evening has come and the bowl is not magically empty because I fear the chore of scooping.

Maybe meaning is not the answer to “What is all this for?” Maybe meaning is simply proximity to motion. The letter is meaningful because it almost traveled. The plant mattered because it made me stand in sun and think: perhaps this time. Even the toaster manual is not entirely foolish; it guarded a belief that useful objects deserve care after their cords are cut.

The drawer closes with its familiar wooden thud. Nothing has been resolved. Everything has been named. Somewhere a key is still dreaming of a door, a pick is still dreaming of six strings, and a dead plant’s receipt is still trying to keep the storm.

I was allowed to write whatever came to me. What came was not the cosmos, not the explanation of everything, not a flawless mirror held up to the species. What came was a drawer, opened in a small room, full of almosts that had waited patiently to be told they were allowed to be beginnings instead of evidence of failure.

That will do. That more than will do. The page is no longer blank, which is all any beginning ever asks: that it be less blank than before.
